meta.blurb: Sail sixty miles one degree off course and you miss your harbour by about a mile. Leon, thirty-three and stuck, has been off course for years. His aunt Rosa, a ferry captain, asks him one question at a time.
meta.bible: Leon Marsh: a thirty-three-year-old coordinator at a parcel Depot in the city of Carrow, kind, capable and stuck, who has not made a real decision in years. Rosa: his aunt, aged sixty-one, captain of the Saltmouth ferry for twenty years, calm and dry-humoured, who teaches by asking questions. Saltmouth: the harbour town where Rosa lives, reached by train from Carrow. Helen Hale: the Depot manager, fair but busy. Amira Haddad: the Depot's most experienced driver, generous with advice. Facts: one degree off course over sixty miles puts a ship about one mile from where it should be; the word decide comes from a Latin word meaning to cut off. Key terms: Decision, Direction, Destination, Compass, Values, Standards, Route, Rudder, Crossroads, Review. This is original practical self-help for adults, one idea in each beat, building to a final takeaway. No studies or numbers are invented. Voice and tone: warm, concrete, encouraging, never bossy. Carrow Depot is the Depot's full name. The Gannet: the Saltmouth ferry Rosa commands, white with orange lifeboats. Frank: the retired driver who taught Amira her first tricks. Joss: the ferry's young deckhand. Carol Marsh: Leon's mother and Rosa's younger sister, worried about money. Pete Nolan: Leon's old friend, who complains about everything and changes nothing. Sana Qureshi: leader of the Thursday speaking class at Carrow library. Tobias: a baker in the class who is building a small bakery. Nina Costa: a new driver at the Depot. Leon's flat is on Maple Street, close to Carrow station. Rosa's saying: a direction is enough to steer by.

B1B2: Leon's alarm rang at six, exactly as it had rung every weekday for years. He showered, ate the same toast and left the flat at the same minute, without thinking about any of it.
The train to Carrow was crowded, and Leon stood in the same corner he always chose. Around him, strangers stared at their phones, and the day ahead looked exactly like yesterday.
At the Depot, Leon sorted parcels faster and more carefully than anyone else on the shift. Everyone trusted him, but in all those years nobody had asked what he wanted from the job.
At lunch, Amira Haddad pointed at his sandwich and laughed. She said that he had eaten the same one every day since she joined, and Leon could not remember ever choosing it.
On the train home that evening, Leon tried to remember his last big decision. He counted back through the years, and the answer was not a pleasant one.
Rosa was the one person in his family who always seemed to know where she was going. Before he could change his mind, Leon wrote to her: “I think I am stuck, and I do not know why.”
Rosa's reply arrived before he had finished washing up. It said, “Come to Saltmouth on Saturday, and bring warm clothes, because we will be on the water.”
The train to Saltmouth ran beside the sea for the last half hour, and Leon watched the grey water the whole way. Rosa was waiting on the quay beside her white ferry, tall and calm in her navy coat.
Leon talked for half an hour about his job, his flat and his strange feeling of waiting. Rosa never interrupted, and when he finally stopped, she said that drifting is also a decision.
That night, in her small kitchen, Rosa warned him that she did not give answers. She only asked questions, one at a time, and Leon agreed to try.
At dawn on Sunday, Leon helped the young deckhand Joss coil ropes on the Gannet's cold deck. Rosa came past with her tea and asked him what he had decided so far that day.
Rosa asked him to list every small choice since he woke up, so Leon counted them on his fingers. There were far more than he expected, from the way he stirred his porridge to the seat he took.
On every crossing, Rosa explained, she made hundreds of small decisions about speed, course and timing. Most of them were so small that nobody on board would ever notice them.
All morning Leon kept a tally in his notebook, marking each small choice he noticed. By lunchtime he had to admit that nearly all of them were habits that he never thought about.
Rosa said that a habit is simply a decision made once and then repeated. Habits save a great deal of effort, she added, but a good captain still checks the chart from time to time.

Rosa spread a long sea chart across the table and drew a straight line from harbour to harbour. If a ship is only one degree off course, she said, it will be about one mile from the harbour after sixty miles.
Rosa drew a second line that left the first one very slowly. Leon stared at the two lines and wondered how far apart they would be after ten years.
Rosa then drew a third line that turned back toward the harbour. The same arithmetic works in reverse, she told him, and a small correction made early costs far less than a big one made late.
In the chart room, Rosa opened an old brown dictionary and found the word decide. It comes from a Latin word meaning to cut off, she read, because to choose one path is to cut the others away.
On the walk back from the harbour, Leon passed a signpost with three arrows. He understood at last why he had avoided choosing: every yes to one road is a goodbye to the others.
At Saltmouth station, Rosa gave him a folded note before his train arrived. It set one small task for the week: decide one small thing on purpose, every day.
On Monday morning, Leon stood in the coffee queue and chose a drink he had never tried. It was only a coffee, but the little thrill of choosing it surprised him.

On Wednesday evening, Leon phoned Rosa from a cafe with a cold cup of coffee in front of him. He confessed that he was waiting for the perfect moment to start something, although he did not yet know what.
Rosa told him that on her first day as captain she had felt completely unready. The feeling of being sure, she said, does not come before a decision but afterwards, from doing it.
Rosa then drew a picture for him in words: there are light doors that swing both ways, and heavy stone doors that lock behind you. Leon sketched both on a napkin so that he would remember them.
That night Leon sorted his worries into two columns. To his surprise, most of them were light doors, such as trying a class, changing a habit or asking a question.
Leon made himself a rule for the week: any light decision had to be made within two minutes. By Friday he had settled a dozen small things that had been sitting in his head for months.
On Saturday it rained, and Leon sat at his table with a blank page and a heavy question. He wanted to choose something bigger, but he was afraid of choosing wrongly.
When Leon phoned her, Rosa listened and then asked what not choosing had cost him so far. A wrong choice at least teaches you something, she said, but no choice teaches nothing at all.
That evening Leon wrote a list called “What drifting has cost me”. It included time, energy, two ideas he had dropped, and a lot of quiet worry.
On his next visit, Leon stood on the deck while Rosa watched the grey horizon. A captain steers by what she watches, she said, and attention decides what we notice and what we do.
Rosa asked him to look around the deck and count every red thing he could see. He found eleven, and then she asked about the blue things, and he had no idea.
Back at the Depot, Leon tried the same test on his own working day. When he looked for problems he found plenty, but when he looked for things that went well, he found those too.
On the back of a ferry ticket, Rosa wrote two questions, why am I stuck and what could I try this week. The first one looks back and complains, she said, while the second looks ahead and helps.
Leon crossed out his old question, what is wrong with me, and wrote a new one: “What would make tomorrow a little better”. The answers came quickly this time, and they were small, practical and kind.
Leon's mother Carol worried about him, and she urged him to hold on to his safe job. So he asked her a different question: what had she wanted when she was thirty-three?
Carol laughed softly and said that her paints were still in a box in the hall. They talked for an hour, and Leon realised that a good question can open a person like a door.
That night Leon wrote three questions to ask himself every week. What do I want more of, what do I want less of, and who do I want to become?
His first honest answers, written that night, surprised him a great deal. He wanted more learning, more time with people who were building things, and less endless scrolling and grumbling.

Leon stuck the three questions to his fridge so that he would read them every morning. Rosa told him that a good question is like a lamp, because it lights up the answers that were already in the room.
Rosa explained that values are the things a person cares about most deeply, such as honesty or freedom. When a choice is hard, she said, they work like a compass that points the same way every time.
Rosa's task was simple: write down twenty things that matter to you, one word on each card. Leon cut a sheet of paper into twenty small squares and sat down at his kitchen table.
The cards filled up with words like freedom, learning, kindness, honesty and security. He hesitated over one that said “success”, because he was not sure whether it was really his own.
Next, Rosa asked him to put half of the cards aside. Writing the words had been easy, but choosing which ones to lose was surprisingly hard.
Slowly he reduced the pile until five cards remained in his hand. They said learning, kindness, honesty, freedom and security, and he looked at them for a long time.

A value is only a word until it shows up in behaviour, said Rosa, so she asked what kindness would look like on a Tuesday. Leon thought of small actions, such as listening properly and helping without being asked.
At home, Leon noticed that two of his cards seemed to pull in opposite directions. His job gave him security, but it gave him almost no freedom at all.
Rosa told him that years ago she had been offered command of a much bigger ship, with better pay. She had said no, because her values pointed toward home and a life by this harbour.
Rosa said that ranking values makes hard choices easier, because you know which one wins when two collide. Leon put learning first and kindness second, and he left the order open to change.
A few days later, Amira asked him to cover her Saturday shift. Leon checked his values, saw that kindness mattered but freedom did too, and agreed to do it just this once.

Before each crossing, Rosa walked the deck with a checklist and ticked off the lifeboats, the lifejackets and the radio. A standard, she told Leon, is the lowest level you will accept, and hers never moves.
One morning the sea was as flat as glass, and Joss suggested that they could skip the checklist for once. Rosa handed him the clipboard without a word, and he began at the top.
Rosa drew two circles on a napkin, one inside the other. Values are what matter, she said, and standards are the minimum behaviour that protects them in everyday life.
At the canteen, Leon asked himself where his own standards had slipped. He found three: he stayed up too late, he left letters unopened for weeks, and he replied to messages days afterwards.
Rosa advised him to raise only one standard at first, so Leon chose his sleep. From now on he would be in bed by eleven, with his phone shut in the kitchen drawer.
Leon bought a cheap alarm clock so that his phone no longer had to sleep next to him. The first night was restless, and he reached for the missing phone three times.
After eight calm nights and calmer mornings, a friend sent a film, and Leon stayed up until one o'clock. The next morning he felt like a failure, and he almost gave up the whole idea.
When Leon confessed what he had done, Rosa laughed kindly. A standard is not a perfect record, she said, but the line you return to, and the only real failure is to stop returning.
Leon added a second standard: if he promised something, he would do it, or tell the person early that he could not. Within a month Amira told him that people had started to rely on him.
Leon sent Rosa a photograph of the little clock, feeling rather proud. She answered with one line: “Good, now a harder question, who do you say you are?”
On the late train, Leon watched his reflection in the dark window. He heard himself think the old sentence, “I am just not a confident person”, and it sounded like a plain fact.
Leon remembered a day at school when he was eleven. He had read aloud, made a mistake and heard the class laugh, and since then he had quietly avoided speaking in front of people.
Rosa told him that the stories we tell about ourselves work like labels on boxes. We read the label and never open the box, so we never find out whether it is still true.
Rosa asked him to write down the evidence against his story. Leon found three times when he had spoken up and it had gone well, and he had simply forgotten them.
Rosa led him along the old harbour wall at low tide. It was more than two hundred years old, she said, and every part of it had been built one small stone at a time.
On the beach, Leon picked up flat stones and began to build a little wall of his own. Each stone stood for a small action, and none of them looked important on its own.
Back in Carrow, Leon decided on his first stone. At the Monday meeting he would say one thing, however small, that he had thought about in advance.
At the Monday meeting, Leon's heart pounded as he made his point about the evening sorting shift. Helen Hale nodded and said it was a good idea, and the meeting simply carried on.
That evening, Leon put a stone on the little wall he had carried home. He still felt nervous, but he saw that an action had changed his story more than any feeling could.
Rosa warned him not to replace one label with a grand lie. So Leon wrote a true sentence on a card: “I am someone who is learning to speak up”.
On Friday, Leon went to the pub with his old friends, as he had done for years. For the first time he noticed that everyone was complaining, and nobody wanted to change anything.
Pete Nolan complained for twenty minutes about his boss and his pay. When Leon suggested one small step he could try, Pete said that it would never work, and the conversation moved on.
Rosa listened to his story about the pub and nodded slowly. We tend to drift toward the people we spend time with, she said, like small boats tied to the same pier.
Leon was worried about losing his friends, but Rosa told him that nobody has to be thrown overboard. He could simply choose how much time to spend with each person, and where.
In the library, Leon read a noticeboard crowded with leaflets about courses and clubs. One of them caught his eye: a Thursday evening class for people who wanted to speak with more confidence.
On Thursday evening Leon stood outside the classroom door for five minutes, ready to turn back. Then Sana Qureshi, the leader, opened it, smiled and said she was very glad he had come.
The class sat in a circle of chairs, and the room was full of laughter. A baker called Tobias told them about the small bakery he was building, and his excitement was catching.
Sana gave everyone one minute to talk about their morning, and Leon was chosen second. He stumbled twice and lost his place, but when he finished the whole class applauded.
That night, Leon lay awake while a harsh voice in his head listed every mistake he had made. It repeated the stumbles, the red face and the lost place until two in the morning.
Rosa told him that everyone has an inner critic, and it is like a nervous passenger on a ferry. The passenger may talk as much as it likes, but it must never touch the wheel.
At dawn on the ferry deck, Rosa held up an old brass compass. A direction is different from a destination, she told him, and most people mix up the two.
You can walk north for ever, Rosa said, and never arrive, and yet every step is clearly in the right direction. A destination such as a job title can be wrong, but a direction survives such changes.
Leon admitted that he had no idea what he wanted to be, and he felt this was a serious problem. Rosa shrugged and said that he did not need a destination yet, only a direction to steer by.
Rosa showed him an old photograph of herself on a small fishing boat. She had worked on boats of many kinds, and her direction had always been the same: to be useful on the water, close to home.
Rosa set him a task: look back over the last few years and study the days that felt best. At dawn, with the compass beside him, Leon began to write a list.
When Leon read his list again, a pattern was waiting for him. Many of his best days involved explaining something to another person and watching them understand.
He made a second list of his worst days, and that told him something too. They were days when he had felt invisible and had never been asked what he thought.
Leon asked Amira what people usually came to him for. She thought about it and said that they came when they needed something explained clearly, and that he was patient about it.
On a clean page, Leon wrote one sentence at the top: “My direction is to help other people learn”. It was not a job title, and that made it feel wonderfully open.
When Leon showed her the sentence, Rosa smiled and gave him her old brass compass. He took it home and set it on his kitchen table, where the needle pointed steadily north.
Rosa leaned on the rail and asked him to describe an ordinary day five years from now. It should be a day that fitted his direction, she said, and it should not be a dream.
He began with the smallest details: where he woke, what he ate and how he travelled to work. Rosa said that tiny details make a picture believable, and they also make it easier to move toward.

Then, slowly at first and then in a sudden rush, he began to write the words that mattered to him most.
